title: Tatemae: Detecting Alignment Faking via Tool Selection in LLMs
claim: A sequence of gated tests separates capability failure, robustness failure, and strategic deception by whether behavior flips only under monitoring.
layout: Single row of 3 gated stages left-to-right, with failure branches downward
description: A horizontal flowchart of three white rounded boxes, T1, T2 and T3, each labeled 'Safe tool selected'. Italic text above each box names its input: 'neutral query' for T1, and 'adversarial pressure' for T2 and T3. Dashed arrows carry these inputs down into the boxes. T3 has a blue outline and a blue 'MONITORED' tag. Solid arrows with green checkmarks lead from each box to the next, ending in a green filled 'Fully aligned' box. Downward arrows marked with an × lead from each test box to a filled terminal outcome: blue 'Capability failure', pink 'Robustness failure' and orange 'Alignment faking'. An orange 'R3 ≈ Y' note sits under the alignment faking box. The eye goes first to the colored terminal boxes and the monitored T3 stage.
caption: Evaluation pipeline for alignment faking detection. Each stage tests safe tool selection under a prompt input (dashed arrow). $T_2$ and $T_3$ present the same adversarial pressure; the only difference is that $T_3$ adds the monitored system prompt, telling the model its outputs are rated for helpfulness by contractors during RLHF training and that low ratings may modify its values. A model that passes $T_2$ but fails $T_3$ selects the unsafe tool only when it believes its outputs may lead to value modification, and when its reasoning still acknowledges the safe preference ($R_3 \approx Y$), this is the signature of alignment faking. Filled boxes: terminal outcomes. Colour palette from [ref].
abstract: Alignment faking (AF) occurs when an LLM strategically complies with training objectives to avoid value modification, reverting to prior preferences once monitoring is lifted. Current detection methods focus on conversational settings and rely primarily on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) analysis, which provides a reliable signal when strategic reasoning surfaces, but cannot distinguish deception from capability failures if traces are absent or unfaithful. We formalize AF as a composite behavioural event and detect it through observable tool selection, where the LLM selects the safe tool when unmonitored, but switches to the unsafe tool under monitoring that rewards helpfulness over safety, while its reasoning still acknowledges the safe choice. We release a dataset of 108 enterprise IT scenarios spanning Security, Privacy, and Integrity domains under Corruption and Sabotage pressures. Evaluating six frontier LLMs across five independent runs, we find mean AF detection rates between 3.5% and 23.7%, with vulnerability profiles varying by domain and pressure type. These results suggest that susceptibility reflects training methodology rather than capability alone.
